title: Trotterisation Thresholds and Dissipative Quantum Chaos in Open-System Digital Quantum Simulation
authors: Angsar Manatuly, Lukas M. Sieberer, Cahit Kargi, Nathan K. Langford
abstract: Digital quantum simulation (DQS) is one of the most promising applications of quantum computing. Trotterised DQS models quantum dynamics by decomposing the evolution into a sequence of gate-based Trotter steps. Using larger Trotter steps reduces the required gate count, but it is now understood that the Trotterisation step size cannot be increased beyond a certain threshold value, beyond which there is a sudden breakdown in simulation accuracy, due to the onset of quantum chaos. To date, this behaviour has only been studied for closed systems not subjected to the environmental noise and decoherence to which real-world quantum computers are highly sensitive. In this work, we study a range of experimentally relevant open-system quantum simulator models and show that Trotterisation thresholds persist even when open-system effects are included, even in the long-time, steady-state limit, once all coherence has been lost. We show that open DQS can accurately reproduce the dynamics of open target systems prior to the threshold, but still exhibits a sudden performance breakdown beyond it. We introduce new, statistical techniques to rigorously characterise the onset of quantum chaos beyond the Trotterisation threshold for both approximately unitary and genuine dissipative quantum chaos, based on random matrix theory (RMT), building on techniques developed for closed systems. Finally, we demonstrate that dissipative quantum chaos emerges when the dissipation is in balance with the presence of underlying unitary quantum chaos; the dissipation must be strong enough to induce genuinely dissipative behaviour, yet not so strong as to suppress the underlying chaotic structure.
summary: This paper analyzes how the breakdown of quantum simulation accuracy, known as the Trotterisation threshold, behaves when environmental noise and decoherence are present. Using three distinct physical models, the authors demonstrate that this threshold persists even in the steady state, confirming that the underlying unitary chaos dictates the simulation limit. They introduce RMT techniques to characterize the emergence of genuinely dissipative quantum chaos.
main_problem: The paper investigates the persistence and nature of the 'Trotterisation threshold' in Digital Quantum Simulation (DQS) when open-system effects (environmental noise and decoherence) are included, and characterizes the emergence of quantum chaos in these open systems.
main_result: The Trotterisation threshold persists even in the long-time, steady-state limit of open systems, and dissipative quantum chaos emerges when dissipation balances underlying unitary quantum chaos.
method: The authors use open-system DQS applied to three models, characterizing chaos using new statistical techniques based on Random Matrix Theory (RMT) applied to both unitary and dissipative regimes.
model_or_system: The study examines open-system quantum simulators using the Lindblad master equation, applied to paradigmatic models including the quantum kicked top, the nearest-neighbour Heisenberg spin chain, and the Rabi model.
key_observables: Spin magnetization ($\langle ar{J}_zangle$), qubit polarization ($\langle\sigma_1^zangle$), normalized photon number ($\langle nangle/n_j$), and simulation fidelity ($F$).
important_parameters: Trotter step size ($	au$), dissipation rates ($\gamma_k$), and the dissipation scaling factor ($f_\gamma$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Markovian dissipation approximation, and the threshold behavior is analyzed across varying dissipation strengths.
figures_summary: Figures show time evolution of observables and fidelity for the three models across varying dissipation strengths and Trotter step sizes, demonstrating the threshold's persistence in both time and steady-state regimes.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the DQS of three open systems, first establishing the persistence of the threshold in time-domain observables, then confirming this in steady-state fidelity measurements, and finally detailing the conditions for dissipative quantum chaos.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it bridges the gap between idealized closed-system quantum chaos theory and realistic open quantum systems, providing crucial diagnostics for assessing the feasibility of quantum simulation in noisy environments.
